answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin’s words — he wrote it about wine, not beer
answer.sourceLine: Franklin really did write a version of this line — but about wine, not beer. In a letter of about 1779 to the French cleric André Morellet he called good wine “a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.” According to Quote Investigator ↗, the familiar “beer” wording is a modern substitution that first surfaced around 1996 and is found nowhere in Franklin’s writings.

source.excerpt: Behold the rain which descends from heaven upon our vineyards, and which incorporates itself with the grapes to be changed into wine; a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy!
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the genuine line in Franklin’s c.1779 letter to the Abbé Morellet — about wine — first printed in the 1818 Memoirs, and dates the “beer” variant to a January 1996 Doylestown, Pennsylvania newspaper item.
The Franklin Institute ↗ lists the beer line among “7 Things Benjamin Franklin Never Said,” noting his wine reflection was reworded into the beer quotation over time.
source.excerptNote: Franklin’s genuine passage, in the English translation printed alongside the French in his grandson’s 1818 Memoirs. Note the subject is wine — the word “beer” appears nowhere in it.

source.rightsNote: The genuine wine passage was written by Franklin around 1779 and first published in 1818 in his grandson’s Memoirs of the Life and Writings of Benjamin Franklin; that early-19th-century text and translation are long in the public domain. The specific “beer” wording, by contrast, is an unsourced modern invention with no original author of record.

author.heading: About Benjamin Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a printer, scientist, diplomat and one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. During his years in France he wrote witty, affectionate letters to friends including the economist and cleric André Morellet — one of which contains his genuine, wine-centered remark that later mutated into the famous beer quotation.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Benjamin Franklin. He wrote it about WINE, not beer — a line from his c.1779 letter to the Abbé Morellet, first published in 1818. The "beer" wording is a 1990s substitution.

misattribution.heading: How a wine line became a beer meme
misattribution.intro: The quotation is real in spirit but wrong in a crucial word. Franklin praised wine; someone later swapped in beer, and the brewed-up version now dominates coasters, T-shirts and bar walls.

items.why: Franklin never wrote about beer here. His genuine line, in a c.1779 letter to the Abbé Morellet, calls wine “a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.” Quote Investigator ↗ could find no support for any beer version before the mid-1990s.

The earliest located beer instance is a January 1996 newspaper item in Doylestown, Pennsylvania about Tun Tavern, per Quote Investigator ↗ — more than two centuries after Franklin’s death, and produced simply by replacing “wine” with “beer.”

misattribution.truthLine: Franklin genuinely wrote the thought — about wine, in a letter to the Abbé Morellet published in 1818; the beloved “beer” wording is a modern substitution, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: Franklin’s wine remark is charming and quotable, and his reputation as a bon vivant made him the perfect magnet for a drinking toast. Swapping “wine” for “beer” localized the sentiment for American beer culture — and craft-beer marketing has kept it in circulation ever since.

Because the underlying line is authentically Franklin’s, the beer version is unusually sticky: fact-checkers have to explain not that the quote is wholly fake, but that a single, load-bearing word was changed.
detailsBody: The genuine passage praises rain becoming wine in the vineyard as evidence of divine goodwill — a poetic conceit, not a literal endorsement of any one drink.
The letter to Morellet is undated in the 1818 Memoirs; it is conventionally placed during Franklin’s diplomatic years in France, around 1779.
context.pull: He said it about wine. The beer is ours.
